body.text: Ketan Parekh's scheme was the 1992 playbook rebuilt for the dot-com era: a handful of favourite stocks, borrowed bank money, and prices set by trades among friends. It ended the same way, with the lenders and ordinary investors left holding the losses.

children.text: In Lesson 2.3 you saw Zee Telefilms triple and then collapse by over 90%. That was not only the dot-com bubble bursting. It was also part of India's second great market scandal. This lesson explains how a broker used a co-operative bank and a private bank to fund a rally in a small group of technology, media and telecom stocks, how a group of short sellers and a payment crisis brought it down in March 2001, and how the damage reached bank depositors and millions of investors in UTI's flagship scheme, US-64.
Who Was Ketan Parekh?

markDefs.definition: An informal name for about ten stocks associated with Ketan Parekh during the 1999 to 2001 boom, mainly in technology, media and telecom, whose prices were allegedly manipulated.

children.text: Ketan Parekh was a Mumbai chartered accountant from a family of stockbrokers. In the late 1990s he became one of the most closely watched operators on Dalal Street, known for backing stocks in the fashionable "ICE" sectors: information technology, communications and entertainment. When he was seen buying a stock, others piled in behind him. His favourite stocks became known as the
K-10 stocks

children.text: How the Scheme Worked

markDefs.definition: Repeatedly buying and selling the same shares among a group of related parties to create an illusion of heavy demand and push up the price, without any real change in ownership.

children.text: Investigations, including by a Joint Parliamentary Committee, described a scheme built on three elements. First,
circular trading

among connected entities created the appearance of heavy demand. Second, large sums were borrowed from banks, notably Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank (MMCB), where Parekh was a director, and Global Trust Bank. Third, the inflated shares themselves were pledged as security for more loans.
Choose stocks with relatively few freely traded shares, so a modest amount of buying moves the price.
Trade shares back and forth among connected entities to lift the price and generate volume that attracts other buyers.

markDefs.definition: A payment instrument issued by a bank, similar to a demand draft, that guarantees payment. Unlike a cheque, it is supposed to be backed by funds already held by the bank.

children.text: Borrow from friendly banks, including through
pay orders
issued without adequate backing, and pledge the now more valuable shares as collateral.
Use the borrowed money to buy more of the same stocks, pushing prices higher still.
Higher prices raise the value of the pledged shares, allowing even more borrowing.
Institutions and retail investors, seeing strong momentum in "new economy" stocks, buy in and provide an exit for anyone who wants to sell.

body.text: Notice the loop. Rising prices increased the collateral, more collateral allowed more borrowing, and more borrowing pushed prices higher. It is the same feedback loop you saw in Lesson 1.3, running upwards. The danger is that the loop works just as powerfully in reverse.

body.caption: A haircut is the discount a lender applies to the value of collateral, to protect itself if prices fall.

body.title: Your Turn: When the Collateral Loop Reverses
body.prompt: An operator pledges shares worth ₹500 crore to a bank that applies a 50% haircut, and borrows the full amount allowed. The pledged shares then fall 60% in value. How much, in ₹ crore, does the operator now need to repay or top up to bring the loan back within the bank's limit?
body.explanation: Original loan = ₹500 crore × 50% = ₹250 crore. After a 60% fall, the shares are worth ₹200 crore, so the bank will lend only ₹100 crore against them. The shortfall is ₹250 crore minus ₹100 crore = ₹150 crore. If the operator cannot find that money, the bank sells the pledged shares, pushing prices down further and shrinking the collateral of everyone else in the same stocks.

body.title: What Does Circular Trading Achieve?
body.question: A group of related entities repeatedly buy and sell the same shares among themselves at steadily rising prices. What is the main purpose?
options: To raise fresh capital for the company
To create an illusion of genuine demand and rising prices that draws in outside buyers
To reduce the company's tax liability
To increase the company's dividend payments
body.explanation: Circular trades do not change who really owns the shares, but they do change what the market sees: rising prices and heavy volumes. Outside investors interpret that as genuine interest and buy in, often at the top. That is why exchanges and SEBI track patterns of trading among connected parties, and why circular trading is treated as manipulation.

children.text: The Bear Cartel and the Payment Crisis

In early 2001, the dot-com bubble was deflating worldwide, and a group of traders, often described as a bear cartel, began aggressively selling K-10 stocks, betting that they would fall. As prices dropped, the collateral loop reversed. Parekh's entities struggled to meet their obligations, and the stress exposed the banks that had funded him.

body.title: The Unravelling of the K-10 Scheme

events.title: The K-10 Rally
events.description: Technology, media and telecom stocks linked to Parekh multiply in price amid the global dot-com boom.

events.title: The Bears Attack
events.description: A group of traders begins heavily selling K-10 stocks. Prices slide as the global technology bust deepens.

events.title: A Nervous Market
events.description: The day after the Union Budget, the Sensex falls 176 points, and the government orders an inquiry into the market's movements.

events.title: The Bank Run Begins
events.description: News spreads that Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank has large exposures to Parekh. Depositors rush to withdraw.

events.title: Payment Crisis in Kolkata
events.description: Parekh defaults on payments to brokers on the Calcutta Stock Exchange, and around 70 brokers default in turn.

events.title: MMCB Shuts Its Doors
events.description: RBI restricts the bank's operations. It later emerges that the bank has lost not only its capital but 96.2% of its deposits.

events.title: Parekh Arrested
events.description: Bank of India files a criminal complaint over ₹137 crore of MMCB pay orders it had discounted for Parekh's firms, and the CBI arrests him.

events.title: The Day of Reforms, and the UTI Freeze
events.description: Compulsory rolling settlement, a ban on the badla carry-forward system and index-based market-wide circuit breakers all take effect. The same day, UTI suspends repurchases in its US-64 scheme for six months.

events.title: The Bottom
events.description: Days after the 11 September attacks, the Sensex hits a low of 2,594.87.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Repeatedly buying and selling the same shares among related parties to fake demand and push up the price is called ___ trading.
body.explanation: Circular trading was central to the K-10 scheme. Exchanges now run surveillance systems that flag unusual trading patterns among connected accounts, and SEBI treats such trading as a fraudulent and unfair trade practice.

children.text: The Damage Spread Far Beyond Traders

body.caption: Who Paid for the K-10 Collapse

cells: Depositors of Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank
The bank lost 96.2% of its deposits. Its licence was finally cancelled in 2012
Bank of India
Discounted ₹137 crore of MMCB pay orders for Parekh's firms that could not be honoured
Shareholders of Global Trust Bank
The bank's problems persisted. RBI imposed a moratorium on 24 July 2004 and merged it with Oriental Bank of Commerce, with nothing for GTB shareholders
UTI US-64 unitholders
About 2 crore investors were hit when repurchases were frozen on 2 July 2001. When UTI disclosed the scheme's NAV for the first time in January 2002, it was about ₹6 per unit
Brokers on the Calcutta Stock Exchange
Around 70 brokers defaulted during the March 2001 payment crisis
Retail investors in K-10 stocks
Many bought near the top and saw losses of 80% to 90% or more

children.text: UTI's losses show how a scheme that ordinary savers believed was safe had been exposed to the same stocks. As of 29 June 2001, UTI's holding in HFCL, one of the K-10 stocks, had cost ₹1,050.70 crore to acquire. Its market value had fallen to ₹87.94 crore.

body.title: Your Turn: UTI's HFCL Loss
body.prompt: UTI acquired HFCL shares at a total cost of ₹1,050.70 crore. By 29 June 2001, they were worth ₹87.94 crore. What percentage of the cost had been lost? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Loss = (1 minus 87.94 ÷ 1,050.70) × 100 = about 91.6%. Money from a scheme that crores of small savers treated as safe had lost more than nine tenths of its value in a single stock. The government later had to step in with support for US-64 investors.

body.label: UTI US-64, 2 July 2001
body.context: US-64 was India's most popular investment scheme, trusted by about 2 crore investors as almost as safe as a bank deposit. The freeze, and the later disclosure of a NAV of about ₹6 per unit, shattered that trust.

children.text: The Reforms After 2001
Where 1992 built the basic infrastructure of a modern market, 2001 tightened the rules around it. Several major reforms took effect on the same day, 2 July 2001.

body.caption: What Changed After the K-10 Crash

cells: Badla let traders carry forward large positions without paying for them
Badla banned and compulsory rolling settlement introduced on T+5 from 2 July 2001
Settlement shortened to T+3 in April 2002, T+2 in April 2003 and T+1 today
No automatic brake on market-wide panic
Index-based market-wide circuit breakers introduced on 2 July 2001
Trading halts at 10%, 15% and 20% moves in the Sensex or Nifty 50
Weak detection of circular trading and price rigging
Stronger exchange surveillance and SEBI investigations
Surveillance frameworks such as ASM and GSM flag unusual price moves
Small banks lending recklessly to brokers
RBI tightened rules on bank lending to stockbrokers and against shares
Bank exposure to capital markets is regulated and capped
Opaque schemes with implied guarantees
UTI restructured and US-64 wound down, with mutual funds held to the same disclosure rules as others
Every mutual fund discloses its NAV daily and its portfolio regularly

body.title: Bulls, Bears and Who Is to Blame

children.text: The 2001 crash is sometimes told as a story of villainous bears destroying a bull operator. The reality is more nuanced.
Short selling is legitimate.
Betting that an overvalued stock will fall is a normal part of a healthy market, and it helps bring prices back towards fair value.
Manipulation is illegal in either direction.
Spreading false rumours or coordinating trades to crash a price is as unlawful as rigging it upwards.
The root cause was the leveraged bull scheme.
Stocks pushed far above their value with borrowed money were always going to fall hard once buying stopped. Short sellers accelerated a collapse that the structure of the scheme made inevitable.

Parekh was convicted in 2008 in one of the cases against him, and SEBI barred him and associated entities from the market for 14 years with effect from December 2003. In January 2025, SEBI issued an interim order barring him again, in an alleged front-running case involving illegal gains of about ₹65.77 crore. He has contested SEBI's allegations in that matter, and proceedings have continued.

body.title: What Is Inside Your Mutual Fund?
body.scenario: Your uncle, a retired teacher, keeps most of his savings in a small cap mutual fund because it returned 45% last year. He thinks mutual funds are "safe because they are regulated". You look at the fund's latest monthly portfolio and see that its top holdings include several small companies whose share prices have risen four to six times in 18 months, some with low trading volumes.
body.prompt: What does the UTI US-64 episode teach about this situation, and what would you check to help your uncle understand the risk?
body.modelAnswer: The US-64 episode shows that a trusted, regulated structure does not make the underlying investments safe. US-64 investors thought they held something close to a bank deposit, but the scheme had bought risky stocks, including K-10 names, and its value collapsed. Today's mutual funds are far more transparent, with daily NAVs, regular portfolio disclosure and SEBI rules, but a small cap fund is still fully exposed to the prices of the small companies it owns. To understand the risk, check: the fund's riskometer label and scheme category; how concentrated the portfolio is in its top ten holdings; whether those holdings have fundamentals, such as sales and profit growth on Screener.in, that support the price rise; the fund's disclosures on liquidity, including how long it would take to sell a large part of its small cap holdings, which fund houses now publish; and how the fund performed in past sharp falls, such as March 2020. Most importantly, look at your uncle's situation: a retiree who may need this money should consider whether a large allocation to small caps matches his need for stability and income. Past returns of 45% say nothing about safety, and very high recent returns in small illiquid stocks can mean higher risk, not lower.

body.title: Check Your Mutual Fund for Hidden Concentration Risk
steps: Download your fund's latest monthly portfolio from the fund house website or AMFI
Add up the weight of the top ten holdings to see how concentrated the fund is
Look up the three largest holdings on Screener.in and compare their price rise with their profit growth
Check the fund's riskometer and scheme category, and whether they match what you thought you owned
For small and mid cap funds, find the fund house's published liquidity or stress test disclosures
Compare the fund's fall with its benchmark index during a past crash, such as March 2020
Decide whether this fund's level of risk suits the purpose of the money invested in it

body.label: AMFI: Mutual Fund Information
body.description: The Association of Mutual Funds in India publishes NAVs and links to scheme information for every fund. Use it to find your fund's factsheet and portfolio disclosures.

cards.definition: About ten stocks, mostly in technology, media and telecom, associated with Ketan Parekh's 1999 to 2001 price manipulation.
Repeated trades among related parties to fake demand and push up prices without any real change in ownership.
A bank-issued payment instrument that guarantees payment. MMCB issued pay orders to Parekh's firms without adequate backing.
The discount a lender applies to collateral value. With a 50% haircut, ₹100 of shares supports only ₹50 of borrowing.
A group of traders coordinating heavy short selling to push prices down. Selling short is legal; coordinated manipulation is not.
An old Indian carry-forward system that let traders defer settlement of positions. Banned from 2 July 2001.
Settling each day's trades a fixed number of days later. India moved from T+5 in 2001 to T+1 today.
UTI's flagship scheme, trusted by about 2 crore investors, whose repurchases were frozen on 2 July 2001.

points: Ketan Parekh's K-10 scheme combined circular trading, bank borrowing and pledged shares to push up a small group of technology, media and telecom stocks
Rising prices increased collateral and allowed more borrowing; when prices fell, the same loop forced selling and created shortfalls banks could not cover
A bear cartel and the global dot-com bust triggered the collapse in early 2001, leading to a payment crisis on the Calcutta Stock Exchange and Parekh's arrest on 30 March 2001
The losses reached far beyond traders: MMCB lost 96.2% of its deposits, Global Trust Bank was later merged away, and UTI froze its US-64 scheme
UTI's HFCL holding lost about 92% of its cost, showing how a "safe" scheme had been exposed to manipulated stocks
On 2 July 2001, India banned badla, introduced rolling settlement and market-wide circuit breakers, the foundations of today's T+1 market
